output.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) have demonstrated modest cognitive and functional benefits in randomized controlled trials of mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease. Anti-amyloid therapies such as lecanemab have demonstrated slowing of clinical decline in biomarker-confirmed early-stage disease but require careful patient selection and MRI monitoring for ARIA. Nonpharmacological interventions including cognitive stimulation, physical exercise, and caregiver support show complementary benefits in long-term follow-up studies.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family

Consider the single case-designated optional biomarker route if biological confirmation would change management or uncertainty remains when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected

FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

key_clinical_evidence: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Yoshiko Tanaka is a 79-year-old right-handed retired seamstress who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her daughter, Keiko, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties that have been worsening over the past two years. Her daughter first became concerned approximately two years ago when she noticed her mother was repeating the same questions within a single phone conversation, something that had never happened before. At first, the family attributed this to loneliness following her husband's death four years ago, but the pattern has steadily worsened. Over the past year, her daughter has discovered unpaid utility bills piled in a drawer, and on one occasion the electricity was briefly disconnected before the daughter intervened and began managing her mother's finances. Mrs. Tanaka, who was known among her friends as an exceptionally skilled seamstress capable of complex pattern work, attempted to mend a neighbor's dress six months ago but became confused by the pattern and abandoned the task, something her daughter describes as unprecedented. She has also stopped attending her weekly senior walking group, telling her daughter she cannot remember the meeting time despite having attended the same session for over five years. Her daughter reports that the refrigerator frequently contains expired food, and she has found the same grocery items purchased multiple times on the same day. Three months ago, Mrs. Tanaka called her daughter in distress because she could not remember how to operate the washing machine she has used for fifteen years. She remains able to dress herself, maintain personal hygiene, and prepare simple meals such as rice and miso soup, though her daughter notes the meals have become much less varied than before. Mrs. Tanaka acknowledges that her memory is not as sharp as it used to be and appears embarrassed when her daughter provides examples. She denies episodes of confusion where she did not recognize family members, visual hallucinations, personality changes, or aggressive behavior. She denies headaches, seizures, falls, tremor, or difficulty swallowing. Her sleep pattern has not significantly changed, and her daughter has not witnessed unusual movements or vocalizations during sleep. Her mood has been somewhat low since her husband's passing, but she denies persistent sadness, anhedonia, or suicidal ideation, and she still enjoys watching historical dramas on television.
